webrtc.webrtcUsesIceStunDiscoverAddresse: WebRTC uses ICE/STUN to discover addresses for peer-to-peer connections. STUN usually uses UDP. If a proxy handles only TCP, candidates may expose another public egress. This page creates only a data channel and does not request camera or microphone permission.
webrtc.udpConnectionlessTransportProtoco: UDP is a connectionless transport protocol. A STUN server returns the public mapped address it observes to the client. This tool uses Google and Cloudflare STUN, collects ICE candidates and compares them with HTTP egress. Local addresses hidden by mDNS are not reported as public IPs.
webrtc.howITellIfThereLeak: How can I tell if there is a leak?
webrtc.differentEgressIndicatesDifferent: Different egress only indicates different UDP and HTTP routes, which may be intentional. Check ISP, region and proxy rules. No public address may mean UDP is blocked or the browser restricted collection; this does not establish safety.
webrtc.howDoIFixALeak: How do I fix a leak?
webrtc.checkUdpForwardingTunTrafficHandl: Check UDP forwarding, TUN traffic handling and IPv6 rules in your client. Firefox can disable media.peerconnection.enabled in about:config; Brave can disable non-proxied UDP. Disabling WebRTC affects video conferencing and similar features, so correcting proxy routing is preferable.
webrtc.whyDoProxyTunModesGiveDifferentRe: Why do proxy and TUN modes give different results?
webrtc.systemProxyVirtualNetworkAdapterM: System proxy and virtual network adapter modes handle different traffic scopes. STUN may be unable to send traffic in some proxy modes, while TUN mode can expose the actual UDP route. Check DNS as well; a single WebRTC result is not a complete privacy audit.

dns.faq.whatText: With a proxy or VPN, name lookups should travel through the tunnel too. If they still go straight to your ISP or system resolver, the ISP can see which domains you visit and you may get answers tailored to a different region than your proxy egress.
dns.faq.howText: The page requests random subdomains from Surfshark, Fastly and BrowserLeaks; their authoritative DNS records which recursive resolver asked. Resolver countries are then compared with the browser's HTTP egress (IPv4 and IPv6). A resolver outside the egress country is flagged as a possible leak.
dns.faq.limitsText: Not necessarily. The comparison works per country: if the proxy and your device are in the same country they cannot be told apart, and anycast public resolvers such as Google or Cloudflare may answer from a neighbouring region. If the browser uses secure DNS (DoH), the result covers only the browser; other apps may still leak.
dns.faq.fixTitle: How do I fix a DNS leak?
dns.faq.fixText: Enable DNS hijacking or fake-ip in your proxy client so lookups resolve remotely, use TUN mode to capture system DNS, check that IPv6 DNS is not bypassing the tunnel, or enable secure DNS (DoH) in the browser over the proxy. Run the check again afterwards.
webrtc.verdictLeak: Found {0} public address(es) that differ from the HTTP egress ({1}). WebRTC may be exposing an egress outside the proxy; ignore this if UDP is split-routed on purpose.
webrtc.ipv6LeakHint: The IPv6 address has no matching HTTP IPv6 egress, which usually means the proxy is not handling IPv6.
webrtc.verdictLocalExposed: The public egress matches the HTTP egress, but WebRTC exposes {0} local address(es) ({1}), which can be used for device fingerprinting.
webrtc.verdictLocalOnly: No public candidate was collected, but WebRTC exposes {0} local address(es) ({1}).
webrtc.faq.mdnsTitle: What are mDNS and local address exposure?
webrtc.faq.mdnsText: Modern browsers replace real local IPs with random .local names (mDNS) by default; this page counts those candidates without revealing the address. If you still see addresses such as 192.168.x.x, the browser is exposing local network details, which is common after granting camera or microphone access or when mDNS obfuscation is disabled.
